idiom_name: for-loop that steps the seed and folds it into the accumulator in the same iteration
implementation_notes: Go has no lazy pipeline and no standard fold, so the hylomorphism is expressed as one loop in which the next state is computed (the coalgebra) and folded into the accumulator (the algebra) before the loop repeats - the intermediate slice or tree is simply never created. Keeping the two steps as named methods or closures preserves the pattern's separation without generics or allocation, and this remains the fastest and most idiomatic form. Choose it by default; a generator is worth packaging only when the unfold itself is the reusable API (see the range-over-func variant).
pitfalls: Building a []int first and folding it afterwards is the two-pass version the pattern removes; only the single loop is the hylomorphism.
Unsigned accumulators wrap silently on overflow in Go - pick the widest type or math/big when the input is not bounded by hand.
Large seed structs are copied on every iteration; keep the seed small or hold it behind a pointer, but do not put slices in it and then mutate them (that reintroduces shared state).

variants.name: iter.Seq generator ranged over by the fold (Go 1.23)
variants.idiom_name: iter.Seq[V] push iterator as the unfold + range loop (or iter.Pull) as the fold
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23 lets a function range over a func(yield func(V) bool) - an iter.Seq - so the unfold becomes an ordinary function value that the consumer drives with a range loop: 'for v := range Countdown(n) { acc *= v }'. Nothing is buffered, because the iterator calls back for each element instead of storing them, so the fusion is preserved while the generator gains an API, composability (slices.Collect, iter.Pull) and compiler checking. Use it when the producer is shared or should be tested on its own; keep the plain loop when the unfold is a one-off arithmetic sequence and the closure would only add indirection.
pitfalls: A yield callback that returns false means the consumer stopped: ignoring the bool keeps generating work nobody wants and can hang a partially consumed pipeline.
iter.Seq values are single-shot push iterators and must not be called concurrently; a second range over the same closure re-runs the producer, which may or may not be acceptable.
Building the same API with a channel plus goroutine allocates and couples the producer to scheduling; range-over-func exists to avoid exactly that.
